strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: reward-guided fine-tuning of diffusion models when rewards are non-differentiable, which is common in biomolecular design.

Proposes a coherent and computationally practical off-policy iterative distillation framework based on value-weighted MLE, avoiding direct reward backpropagation and reducing reliance on on-policy PPO-style updates.
Evaluates the method on a diverse set of scientific tasks, including protein sequence/structure design, regulatory DNA design, and small-molecule docking, with multiple baselines and reward metrics.
Provides implementation details, hyperparameter tables, and additional results/ablations, including combinations with inference-time Best-of-N sampling.
Some empirical results are promising, especially for protein binding tasks, where VIDD improves ipTM and pLDDT over DDPO and other baselines.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the core method is essentially value-weighted maximum likelihood / advantage-weighted regression adapted to diffusion models with lazy target updates; the soft value approximation via one-step denoised prediction is also used in prior test-time guidance work.

Theoretical support is limited: no convergence or performance guarantee is provided for the iterative distillation procedure with approximate value functions, and the forward-vs-reverse KL stability claim is largely empirical rather than rigorously established.

Evaluation has important weaknesses: naturalness/diversity trade-offs are poor on some tasks (e.g., DNA 3-mer correlation is much lower than DRAKES/SFT/DDPP; protein diversity drops substantially), ATAC-Acc has very large uncertainty, and statistical significance is not rigorously assessed.
Some claims appear stronger than the evidence, such as robustness to reward over-optimization on DNA despite high variance and only comparable independent ATAC-Acc performance.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete or potentially under-tuned: Best-of-N is an inference-time method rather than a fine-tuning baseline, DRAKES is only compared on DNA and is not directly applicable to non-differentiable rewards, and stronger recent diffusion RL/alignment baselines are missing.

Reproducibility and clarity issues remain: the code link is omitted in the manuscript, notation around roll-in/roll-out/value approximation is inconsistent, and there are typos/algorithmic details such as the ambiguous `S%K=0` update condition.

strengths: Targets an important and practically relevant problem: fine-tuning diffusion models for non-differentiable reward functions in biomolecular design.
Proposes an intuitive three-phase iterative distillation framework (roll-in, roll-out, distillation) that connects to value-weighted MLE and off-policy RL ideas.
Empirically evaluates on diverse tasks including protein, DNA, and small-molecule design, with comparisons to several baselines (DDPO, DDPP, SFT, Best-of-N, DRAKES).
Reports results across multiple metrics, including reward, naturalness, and diversity, and includes some ablations on roll-in mixture and lazy update interval.
Discusses broader impact and limitations, including ethical concerns around biomolecular generation.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method largely combines existing ideas from value-weighted MLE/advantage-weighted regression, off-policy RL, and test-time diffusion guidance, with incremental adaptation to biomolecular design.

The central soft-value approximation, approximating v_{t-1}(x) by r(hat{x}_0(x)), is not theoretically justified: v_{t-1} is α log E[exp(r/α)|x_{t-1}], not the reward at the posterior mean. This ignores reward variance and can substantially bias the weights, yet no ablation compares it against Monte Carlo or learned value functions.

There is a mismatch between the derivation and the algorithm: the derivation samples x_{t-1} from p^pre, but Algorithm 1 samples from the roll-out policy p^out and uses v^out; the resulting objective is not clearly the stated forward-KL distillation objective.

Theoretical claims about PPO/reverse KL versus forward KL are oversimplified and not fully rigorous; the PPO equivalence has sign/constant issues in the main text and does not substantiate the practical stability claims.

Evaluation is not sufficiently convincing for a top-tier venue: baseline hyperparameters/tuning protocols are largely unspecified, multiple random seeds are not clearly reported, and stability/sample-efficiency claims are not quantitatively measured.

The claimed off-policy and mode-collapse advantages are partially contradicted by results: VIDD often achieves high reward at substantially reduced diversity and worse naturalness (e.g., DNA 3-mer correlation 0.162 vs. 0.879 for DDPP; protein binder diversity 0.52 vs. 0.90 for pre-trained).

Reproducibility and algorithmic details are incomplete: source code is advertised but not linked, β_s schedule is not specified, notation for values/roll-out is inconsistent, and Algorithm 1 contains a clear typo (S%K rather than s%K).
Naturalness/over-optimization is not fully addressed, especially for DNA where reward-model exploitation may occur despite the additional ATAC-Acc metric.
Writing quality needs substantial improvement: numerous typos, duplicated references, undefined symbols, and unclear transitions make parts of the manuscript difficult to follow.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: reward-guided fine-tuning of diffusion models for biomolecular design, where reward functions are often non-differentiable.

The proposed VIDD framework is clearly motivated and reasonably novel: it casts fine-tuning as iterative distillation of soft-optimal policies, using off-policy roll-in, value-guided roll-out, and forward KL minimization.
Provides a useful theoretical connection (Theorem 1) between PPO-style diffusion fine-tuning and reverse KL divergence, helping explain why forward-KL/value-weighted distillation may be more stable.

Broad empirical validation across protein sequence design, protein binder design, DNA enhancer design, and small-molecule docking; VIDD generally improves reward metrics over SFT, DDPO, DDPP, and Best-of-N baselines.
Includes useful ablations on roll-in mixture, lazy update interval, and combination with inference-time techniques, as well as additional naturalness/diversity metrics in the appendix.
The posterior-mean approximation for soft values is computationally efficient and avoids training an additional value network, which is practical for expensive biomolecular reward functions.
Code is released, hyperparameters are documented, and broader impact/limitations are discussed.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core objective is value-weighted maximum-likelihood/off-policy distillation, which is well known in RL, and the soft-value approximation largely follows existing test-time guidance heuristics rather than introducing a fundamentally new algorithmic principle.

The soft value approximation v_{t-1}(x) ≈ r(denoised x) is crude and lacks strong theoretical justification in the fine-tuning setting. The exponential weights in the objective are unnormalized and may be numerically unstable; no convergence, variance, or sample-complexity analysis is provided.

Evaluation has unresolved concerns. Protein diversity drops substantially for VIDD, possibly indicating mode collapse despite the stability claims. DNA 3-mer correlation is much lower than SFT/DDPP, suggesting possible reward overoptimization or reduced naturalness. For protein binding, pLDDT is both part of the reward and reported as a naturalness metric, so it is not independent.

The paper claims improved sample efficiency but does not provide direct comparisons of reward-function calls, wall-clock time, or sample complexity against baselines. This weakens the central practical claim.

Baseline tuning and fairness are not fully established. It is unclear whether DDPO/DDPP were tuned comparably, DRAKES is only included for DNA, and several relevant RL/test-time fine-tuning methods are discussed but not empirically compared.

Derivations and algorithmic presentation have clarity issues. The pseudocode contains a typo ('S%K=0' should likely be 's%K=0'), the roll-out/target update ordering is ambiguous, and the appendix uses a handwavy 'slight abuse' to move from the derived objective to the practical objective.

The forward-KL interpretation is not exact in the implemented off-policy, value-weighted form; the paper does not rigorously quantify the gap between the true forward KL objective and the practical loss.
Broader-impact discussion acknowledges biosafety risks but remains brief given the paper's focus on biomolecular design; more concrete safeguards or dual-use discussion would be desirable.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: reward-guided fine-tuning of diffusion models for biomolecular design, where reward functions are often non-differentiable.

Proposes an off-policy iterative distillation framework (VIDD) that can optimize arbitrary reward functions without requiring differentiable rewards, making it suitable for scientific domains such as protein, DNA, and molecule design.
Leverages forward KL minimization and value-weighted MLE, with a useful conceptual comparison to PPO-style methods that optimize reverse KL.
Provides empirical evidence across three biomolecular domains (protein, DNA, small molecule) with multiple baselines, showing improved reward optimization in several tasks.

Includes numerous ablations and analyses (lazy update interval, regularization coefficient, roll-in mixture, soft value function approximation, noise robustness, combination with Best-of-N), which help clarify design choices.
The paper is generally well written, clearly motivated, and the method is described with sufficient algorithmic detail for implementation.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method combines existing ideas such as soft-optimal policies, value-weighted maximum likelihood / advantage-weighted regression, lazy target updates, and posterior-mean value approximation (used in prior test-time guidance work). The theoretical contribution (connecting PPO to reverse KL) is also largely standard.

Central claims about improved training stability and sample efficiency are not directly measured. There is no quantitative comparison of sample efficiency (e.g., number of reward evaluations), variance across seeds, or convergence speed against baselines. Stability claims rely mostly on training curves and reward-diversity scatter plots.

Evaluation has concerning trade-offs. On DNA enhancer design, VIDD achieves high Pred-Activity but has a much lower 3-mer correlation (0.162 vs 0.887 for DRAKES and 0.879 for DDPP), suggesting a substantial distribution shift from natural sequences. On protein binder design for IFNAR2, diversity drops to 0.52 compared with 0.72 for DDPO and 0.89 for DDPP, raising possible mode-collapse concerns that are not fully resolved.

There are reporting inconsistencies: the main table lists DRAKES with Pred-Activity 6.44, while the appendix distinguishes DRAKES (5.61) and DRAKES w/o KL (6.44), making it unclear which baseline is actually in the main comparison. Reward definitions for protein SS-match are also ambiguous: pLDDT is described as part of the reward in the main text but omitted from the reward definition in the hyperparameter table.

The soft value function approximation is heuristic and lacks theoretical guarantees; the algorithm replaces the true value with r(hat{x}_0) and uses lazy target updates without convergence analysis. This is a notable gap given the iterative distillation framing.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is high. Performance varies substantially with lazy update interval K, regularization coefficient alpha, and roll-in mixture beta, with different optimal values across tasks. This makes the method less turnkey and potentially difficult to reproduce or tune in new domains.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete and their tuning is unclear. Strong inference-time/guidance baselines such as SVDD are only partially compared (mainly in the appendix for molecule generation) and not systematically in the main tables. It is also unclear whether DDPO/DDPP were tuned as carefully as VIDD.

Naturalness and validity metrics are mixed. In molecule generation, VIDD improves docking and NLL but has lower molecule stability and atom stability than DDPO, indicating that reward gains may come with some loss of chemical quality.

The paper reports median reward (50% quantile) rather than mean reward and does not include statistical significance testing, which can make reward comparisons harder to interpret, especially for heavy-tailed reward distributions.
No code or public implementation is mentioned, limiting reproducibility despite the detailed hyperparameter tables.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: reward-guided fine-tuning of diffusion models for biomolecular design where reward functions are often non-differentiable.

The proposed VIDD algorithm is clearly motivated and methodologically plausible, combining off-policy roll-in, soft-optimal teacher policies, and value-weighted maximum likelihood in a coherent iterative procedure.

The experimental evaluation covers multiple biomolecular domains (protein sequence design, regulatory DNA design, and small-molecule design) and includes several relevant baselines such as DDPO and DDPP.

Some empirical results are encouraging, e.g. improvements over DDPO/DDPP on IFNAR2 binder ipTM, molecule docking score, and pLDDT for SS-match, and favorable distributional metrics for molecules in Table 12.
The appendix includes useful additional analyses such as lazy-update ablations, regularization-coefficient sensitivity, value-estimation comparisons, and reward-noise robustness tests.
The paper discusses limitations and broader impact, including potential misuse in biomolecular design.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the method is essentially an application of value-weighted MLE / advantage-weighted regression to diffusion fine-tuning, with soft-optimal policy distillation. The core algorithmic ingredients are largely known, and the paper does not sufficiently distinguish its contribution from existing off-policy reward-weighted or posterior-prediction approaches such as DDPP.

The central claims of improved stability and sample efficiency are not empirically supported. There is no reward-call or sample-efficiency comparison, no stability/variance-across-seeds analysis, and no direct ablation isolating the effect of off-policy updates versus forward KL versus other design choices. The comparison to DDPO conflates multiple differences, so the attributed benefits of off-policy learning and forward KL minimization remain unverified.

The theoretical analysis contains a serious sign error. Theorem 1 in the main text states that the PPO-style objective equals a positive KL divergence, whereas the appendix derivation indicates it equals the negative KL divergence up to a constant. This undermines the claimed reverse-KL interpretation and the theoretical motivation for the method.

The soft value function approximation is heuristic and potentially biased: replacing α log E[exp(r/α)] with r(hat x0) is not theoretically justified and may lead to high-variance or poorly calibrated weights, especially given the sensitivity to α observed in the appendix. No clipping or robust weighting scheme is discussed.

Evaluation is not sufficiently rigorous. Many reported gains are small relative to standard errors, error bars often overlap, and no significance tests or confidence intervals for differences are provided. Several metrics have very large uncertainty (e.g., DNA ATAC-Acc for VIDD: 0.820 ± 0.384), making strong claims unsupported.

Important baselines are missing or unevenly applied. Inference-time guidance methods such as SVDD/SMC are discussed but not compared for reward maximization in most tasks; DRAKES is only evaluated on DNA; the DNA DRAKES row in Table 1 appears inconsistent with Table 8 and omits the full DRAKES/GLID2E results.

Naturalness/validity evidence is weak in places. For DNA, VIDD achieves much lower 3-mer correlation than baselines (0.162 vs. 0.879 for DDPP, 0.887 for DRAKES), and the paper dismisses this as novel exploration without wet-lab or independent functional validation. For molecules, DDPO has better molecule/atom stability than VIDD, and the trade-offs are not fully analyzed.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, the roll-in mixture parameter β_s is not specified in the main experiments, and key hyperparameters/validation procedures are unclear. The algorithm listing also contains minor inconsistencies (e.g., S%K versus s%K).

The significance for real biomolecular design is unclear. The evaluation relies entirely on proxy rewards and computational metrics, with no experimental validation, and there is limited evidence that the method avoids reward overoptimization in practice.

Clarity and presentation need improvement: there are typos, incomplete sentences, inconsistent notation (e.g., roll-out value notation, x_{t-1} samples), and some claims are stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: reward-guided fine-tuning of diffusion models for biomolecular design with potentially non-differentiable rewards.

Proposes a coherent off-policy iterative distillation framework (VIDD) that leverages soft-optimal denoising policies and value-weighted MLE, avoiding on-policy PPO instability and reverse-KL mode-seeking behavior.
Provides a useful theoretical connection between PPO-style objectives and reverse KL divergence, clarifying the motivation for forward-KL-based distillation.
Empirical evaluation spans protein, DNA, and small-molecule design tasks, with improvements over DDPO, DDPP, standard fine-tuning, and Best-of-N on many reward metrics.
Includes informative ablations on roll-in mixture, lazy update interval, regularization coefficient, soft-value approximation, and noisy reward settings.
Reproducibility details are generally strong: algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameter tables, hardware/software, task definitions, and license considerations are provided.
Acknowledges broader ethical implications and limitations, including reward overoptimization and expensive reward evaluation.
weaknesses: Evaluation leaves open the concern of reward overoptimization: for protein SS-match and molecule docking, the optimized reward and reported evaluation metric are essentially the same or closely related, and no held-out reward model is used except in the DNA ATAC-Acc evaluation. This makes it difficult to tell whether VIDD discovers genuinely better designs or exploits the reward proxy.

Important related baselines are missing or only partially compared. Inference-time soft-value/SMC methods such as SVDD, SMC, and DPS are discussed but not compared on reward in the main tables, even though VIDD uses a similar posterior-mean value approximation. Best-of-N alone is not sufficient for this class of methods.

Statistical rigor is limited: the reported ± values appear to be sample-level uncertainty rather than variation across independent training runs, and there is no clear evidence that results are stable across random seeds. This is especially important for RL-style diffusion fine-tuning.

Hyperparameter selection is not fully transparent. Different lazy update intervals and α values are used per task, but it is unclear whether these were selected on validation data with the same budget as baselines. This risks favoring VIDD in the comparisons.

Diversity and naturalness trade-offs are not fully resolved. VIDD substantially reduces diversity in some tasks (e.g., IFNAR2 and SS-match), and on DNA it has much lower 3-mer correlation than DRAKES/DDPP/SFT, suggesting a notable distribution shift. The claim of robustness to overoptimization is only partially supported.

The theoretical presentation has some inconsistencies: the main text states Theorem 1 as J(θ) = reverse KL, while the appendix derives equality only up to a negative sign/constant; the algorithm also contains a likely typo (`S%K=0` instead of `s%K=0`).

Novelty is incremental: the method combines known ingredients such as value-weighted MLE/AWR, soft-optimal diffusion policies, and iterative distillation. The paper does not provide new convergence guarantees under approximate value functions, and the practical algorithm relies on a heuristic posterior-mean value estimate.

Some experimental details and metrics are under-specified, including DDPO/DDPP hyperparameters, number of generated samples, and validation protocols. There are also several citation/reference formatting errors.
